transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi, thank you for seeing me. Um, honestly, I'm here mostly because my sleep has just gotten so incredibly unreliable lately, and it's starting to really take a toll on me. I mean, I work as a sales manager, and it's a demanding job, I completely get that, but it's like I can't leave it at the office anymore. I'll get into bed at night, and I am just physically exhausted—like, bone-tired, completely drained from the day—but the second my head hits the pillow, I just lie there. My mind just starts racing, replaying all the quarterly forecasts, going over the numbers, or I'm analyzing these little team issues and who said what in the afternoon meeting and how I should have handled it. And it just goes on and on. 

Then, if I do finally manage to drift off, it's like my body has a built-in alarm clock for the absolute worst time, because I'll wake up around 3 or 4 in the morning, pretty much without fail. And once I'm awake at that hour, that's it. I just cannot get my brain to power down again. I just lay there in the dark, tossing and turning, completely wide awake while the rest of the world is sleeping, thinking about everything I have to do the next day, and it's just... it's driving me absolutely crazy. I just can't keep functioning on this little rest.
Do you feel overwhelmed or anxious during the day, outside of when you're trying to sleep?

Oh, absolutely. I mean, it's not just the nights, the days are honestly just as bad, maybe worse in some ways because I'm actually supposed to be productive. It's like my brain is on this constant treadmill, and someone just keeps cranking up the speed, you know? Most days, my mind just jumps from one thing to the next, almost without me even realizing it's happening. I'll be sitting at my desk, and I'll start worrying about whether we're actually going to hit our launch numbers for the new quarter. And then, before I've even figured that out, I'm suddenly stressing about my team. Like, Sarah seemed a little quiet in the morning huddle, is she unhappy? Is she about to quit? Because if she quits, we're so short-staffed, and training someone new right now would be a disaster. 

And then it doesn't even stay at work. It bleeds into my personal life, too. I'll suddenly start panicking about the mortgage payment, even though it's on auto-pay and we're fine, but what if something goes wrong with the bank? Or I'll think about a client renewal that isn't even due for three months, but I'm already imagining them walking away. It just feels like every single small delay or tiny hiccup could turn into something major, like this massive catastrophe. If an email takes an hour longer to get a reply to than usual, I'm convinced the deal is dead. It's just exhausting, being on high alert like that all day long, jumping from one worst-case scenario to another. I just can't seem to turn it off, no matter how much I try to just focus on the task in front of me.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain situations or tasks because of your worries or anxiety?

I don't... I don't really think I avoid things, no. I mean, I still go to all my meetings, I still make all my calls, I still do the performance reviews, even though I might be agonizing over them for days beforehand. It's not like I'm hiding under my desk or calling in sick. Actually, it's almost the opposite? Like, because I'm so worried about everything falling apart, I feel like I have to be involved in *everything*. 

Like last week, my assistant was supposed to handle this really straightforward vendor contract, something she's done a million times, but I just couldn't let it go. I kept hovering, asking to see drafts, checking her emails, because I was so terrified she'd miss a clause and we'd be locked into some terrible rate for a year. So I didn't avoid it, I probably over-involved myself. And I do that with my team, too. I'll take on their overflow work instead of just letting them figure it out, because if I do it, at least I know it's done and I don't have to sit there wondering if they're going to drop the ball. 

So, yeah, I'm definitely not avoiding work or situations. I'm just... I'm white-knuckling my way through them, I guess. I'm there, I'm doing the things, but my stomach is in knots the entire time. But I show up. I always show up. I just can't seem to step back and let things happen without feeling like I need to control every single variable to prevent a disaster.
Have you ever found yourself wishing you could avoid a particular task or situation because of how anxious it makes you feel?

Well, wishing I could avoid things? Oh, sure, absolutely. I mean, all the time. Like, internally, I am screaming to just run away from half the things on my calendar. Just looking at my schedule for the week on a Sunday night—which, by the way, I know I shouldn't do, my husband tells me all the time to just close the laptop, but I can't help it—just looking at it makes my chest feel tight. I'll see a one-on-one scheduled with my regional director, and immediately, my brain is just like, "Cancel it. Tell him you're sick. Tell him you have a family emergency." Just this overwhelming urge to escape the situation because I'm already anticipating that he's going to grill me about the Q3 projections, which, honestly, are looking a little soft right now because of supply chain issues that I can't even control, but I know it's going to fall on me. 

So, yes, the *wish* to avoid it is definitely there. I'll sit in my car in the parking garage before work sometimes, just gripping the steering wheel, thinking, "What if I just put it in reverse and drove back home? What if I just got back in bed and pulled the covers over my head?" I play out that entire scenario in my head, just imagining the relief of not having to face the emails, the calls, the constant pressure of everyone needing an answer from me *right now*. It sounds so nice, just for a minute, to disappear from it all. 

But, like I said, I don't actually do it. I never do. I just sit there, feeling sick to my stomach, wishing I could be anywhere else, and then I turn off the car, grab my bag, and walk into the building. Because the anxiety of *not* doing the thing—the guilt, the fear of getting fired, the worry about letting my team down—is somehow even worse than the anxiety of just pushing through it. So I don't avoid it, but boy, do I spend a lot of time wishing I had a magic button to just make it all go away. It's just this constant battle in my head between wanting to hide and feeling like I have to control everything.
Do you feel like your anxiety has caused you to change your daily routines or activities in any way?

Well, changing my routines... I mean, I guess it’s more that it’s changing how I function within those routines. It’s really started affecting both my work and my home life in a big way. Like I was saying about not avoiding things, I still do my job, but the way I do it is just so much harder now. 

Take my pipeline reviews, for example. I used to just go in, look at the numbers, make a call on where we stood, and move on to the next thing. But lately? I spend so much time second-guessing every single decision. I’ll stare at a forecast and think, "Wait, is this rep overly optimistic? Did I miss a red flag in that client email? Should we adjust the projection down by ten percent just to be safe?" And because my brain is doing all of that, the actual review meetings have gotten so incredibly tense. I can feel it in the room. My team is just sitting there, waiting for me to give the green light, and I’m just spinning my wheels, asking them a million tiny follow-up questions that I probably don't even need the answers to, just trying to feel absolutely certain before I commit to a number. It drags everything out and makes everyone, including me, totally miserable.

And then, because I’ve spent eight or ten hours doing *that*—just burning through all this mental energy over-analyzing and worrying and trying to control every little detail—by the time I actually get in my car and drive home, I am just completely depleted. I mean, totally drained. I used to come home, ask my husband about his day, maybe we’d cook dinner together or go for a walk. But now, I walk through the door and I have absolutely nothing left in the tank. 

And I'm so reactive, too. If he asks me a simple question, like "What do you want for dinner?" or "Did you see the mail?", I just snap at him. I don't mean to, but my brain just cannot handle one more decision or one more thing to manage. So instead of spending quality time with him, I just kind of collapse on the couch and zone out. I'm just not fully present with him at all anymore. He'll be talking to me about his day, and I'm just staring at the wall, half-listening, probably worrying about a contract I left on my desk. Which, of course, makes me feel incredibly guilty, because he doesn't deserve that, and then I start worrying that I'm ruining my marriage, which just starts the whole anxiety cycle all over again. So, yeah, I haven't stopped doing my daily activities, but the way I'm functioning during them... it's just really taking a toll on everything.
Are there any specific things, like places, objects, or people, that make you feel anxious?

I mean, when you say specific things, like objects or places... no, not really. It's not like I walk into a specific room and suddenly feel panicked, or like I'm terrified of elevators or dogs or something like that. I actually have a friend who is terrified of bridges, like she will literally drive an hour out of her way to avoid the main highway bridge, but for me, it's nothing like that at all. 

It's more like... it's just a constant hum in the background of everything I do. It doesn't really matter if I'm at the office, or in my car, or sitting on my own couch at home. The anxiety is just there, regardless of my location. It's not triggered by a physical *thing*. It's triggered by my own thoughts, I guess? Like, I could be looking at a completely normal object, like my cell phone, and it's not the phone itself that makes me anxious, it's the spiral of thoughts about who might be emailing me, or what crisis is waiting in my inbox, or if my regional director is trying to get ahold of me about those Q3 numbers I mentioned earlier. 

And it's not specific people, either. I mean, sure, interacting with my boss can be stressful, but I feel just as wound up when I'm talking to my assistant, or my team, or even just sitting entirely alone in my office with the door closed. Or with my husband, like I was saying before. He certainly doesn't make me anxious—he's wonderful, he really is—but I'll be sitting right next to him at the dinner table and my brain is just a million miles away, worrying about a dozen different work scenarios that haven't even happened yet. 

So, yeah, if you're asking if there's a specific trigger, like a certain place I can't go or an object I can't be around... no. I kind of wish it were that simple, honestly. If it was just one thing, like spiders, I could just hire an exterminator or stay away from the woods, you know? But because it's just... life, and my responsibilities, and this constant fear of dropping the ball on literally anything... I can't really escape it by just avoiding a specific place or person. It just comes with me wherever I go.
Do you feel anxious when you're interacting with other people?

Well, it's not the interaction itself, if that makes sense. I mean, not because of the actual interacting part. I'm a sales manager, so my entire career is basically built on talking to people. If I were afraid of talking to people, I would definitely be in the wrong profession! I'm on calls with clients all day, I'm doing one-on-ones with my reps, I'm presenting to the regional directors... I can talk to a brick wall. So it's not like I get butterflies because I have to say hello to someone or because I'm worried about making small talk at a networking event. It's not that kind of social panic where I'm worried people are judging me or anything like that. 

But... am I anxious *while* I'm interacting with them? Yes, absolutely, but that's really just because I'm anxious all the time anyway, like I was saying before. It's the background noise. Like, I could be sitting across from one of my best account executives—someone I've known for five years, totally comfortable with him as a person, we joke around all the time—and I'm still sitting there with my stomach completely tied in knots. But I'm not anxious about *him*. I'm anxious about the fact that his territory is underperforming this quarter, and while he's talking to me about his weekend, I'm running through fourteen different scenarios in my head about how I'm going to explain his numbers to my boss on Friday. 

So I'm nodding, and I'm smiling, and I'm saying all the right things in the conversation, but internally I'm just vibrating with stress about the actual work. Or like with my husband, I'm interacting with him, but the anxiety is about the emails I haven't answered, not about talking to him. So, no, people don't make me anxious just by being people. It's not the socializing. It's just that my brain never shuts off the worrying, no matter who happens to be standing in front of me. I could be chatting with the barista at the coffee shop about the weather, and I'd still be stressing about my pipeline forecast, you know?
Have you started to avoid certain tasks or situations because they might trigger or worsen your anxiety?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I kind of touched on this a little bit earlier, but I really don't avoid things. It’s almost like... I don't even have the luxury of avoiding anything, you know? If I started putting off tasks at work just because they made me stressed, my entire department would completely fall apart. I have a team of reps relying on me, I have regional directors breathing down my neck for those Q3 numbers, so I can't just hide under my desk, as much as I might want to sometimes. 

So, no, I don't avoid the situations. I still open every single email, I still run every single pipeline review, I still have all the hard conversations. It's actually almost the exact opposite of avoiding them, if that makes sense? Because instead of walking away, I force myself to sit there and just grind through it, but I end up over-doing it. Like, I’ll sit at my computer and agonize over a simple forecast spreadsheet for two hours when it should take twenty minutes, just double and triple-checking everything because I'm so worried about getting it wrong or missing something crucial. 

It would probably be a relief to just avoid it and say, "Oh, I'll deal with this tomorrow," but my brain just won't let me do that either. The worry about *not* doing the task is just as bad as the worry *during* the task. I just keep showing up and doing all my daily tasks, I just do them while feeling absolutely miserable and vibrating with stress the entire time. So, yeah, no avoidance, just... just a lot of pushing through it, I guess, even though it exhausts me.
Do you feel like your anxiety would decrease if your work-related stressors were to be significantly reduced?

You would think so, right? I mean, logically, if you take away the biggest source of stress, the stress itself should go down. My husband actually said exactly that to me last week—he suggested I take a step back, maybe look for a less demanding role, or at least take a proper vacation. But honestly? I really don't think it would make a difference. Because it’s not just the actual, tangible work tasks that are the problem. It’s how my brain connects literally everything together into this massive, unending web of panic. 

Like, most days my mind jumps from whether we'll hit the launch numbers to whether someone on my team is about to quit, and then it suddenly skips over to worrying about the mortgage, or a client renewal that isn't even up for another six months. It’s like a pinball machine in my head. I'll be looking at a completely standard sales report and suddenly I'm convinced we're going to lose the house, which is completely ridiculous because we're totally fine financially, but my brain just goes there anyway. 

So even if you took the regional directors and the pipeline forecasts away, I feel like I would just fill that empty space with something else to agonize over. Because the fundamental problem is that it feels like every small delay could turn into something major. If a client takes an extra day to reply to an email, it’s not just a delay—it’s a sign that they’re backing out, which means my rep will miss quota, which means they’ll get demoralized and quit, which means I’ll get fired. It’s always catastrophic. So, no, I don't think reducing the work would fix it, because the worrying itself... it just has a life of its own at this point, no matter what I'm actually supposed to be focusing on.
Do you feel like your anxiety is focused on specific areas of your life, such as work, or is it more general and affects everything you do?

Well, it definitely feels like it affects everything, yeah. I mean, I know I talk about work a lot because, well, that's where I spend most of my time, and as a sales manager, there's always a fire to put out. But it's really not just work. It's like... it's like this general cloud that just hovers over everything I do. I was kind of saying this before, but most days my mind just jumps from one thing to the next, like a monkey swinging on vines, you know? 

I'll start out worrying about whether we're going to hit the launch numbers for the new product line, which is a normal work thing to worry about, sure. But then, almost immediately, I'm worrying about whether someone on my team is about to quit because they seemed a little quiet on the morning zoom call. And then, before I've even resolved that thought, my brain just skips right over to worrying about the mortgage, even though we literally just paid it and we have plenty of savings. Or I'll suddenly start stressing over a client renewal that isn't even up for another six months. It's just constant. 

And it's not even just big things! It's like my brain takes any tiny little detail and blows it up into a disaster. It feels like every small delay could turn into something major. Like, if my husband says he's going to be ten minutes late getting home, I'm not just thinking, "Oh, traffic is bad." I'm thinking, "He got in a car accident, he's in the hospital, I'm going to be a widow, how will I pay for the funeral?" It sounds so crazy when I say it out loud, but in the moment, it feels completely real and terrifying. So, yeah, it's definitely not just focused on work. It just bleeds into literally every single part of my life, all day long.
Do you feel like your anxiety is interfering with your ability to enjoy or participate in activities that you normally like to do?

Well, yeah, absolutely. I mean, it’s not even just about enjoying things anymore, it’s about whether I can even function normally in my day-to-day life, which... honestly, I’m barely managing. It’s started affecting my work and my home life in a really noticeable way. Like, at work, I used to be so decisive. I’m a sales manager, right? You have to make quick calls. But lately, I spend so much time second-guessing every single decision. I’ll sit there staring at the data, wondering if I missed some tiny variable that’s going to ruin the entire quarter. And because of that, our pipeline reviews have become so incredibly tense. My team can feel it. I can see them looking at me, waiting for me to just make a call, and I’m just spinning my wheels, terrified of making the wrong choice. It’s exhausting for them, and it’s exhausting for me.

And then, because I’ve spent the entire day completely wound up, vibrating with all this nervous energy and overthinking every email and every spreadsheet, by the time I actually get home... I’m just totally drained. Like, completely empty. My husband will want to talk about his day, or maybe suggest we watch a movie or go for a walk, which are things I usually love doing with him, but I just... I can’t. I’m so depleted that I just sit there on the couch, completely zoned out. Or worse, I’m reactive. If he asks me a simple question like what I want for dinner, I’ll snap at him because my brain just cannot handle one more decision, even a small one. I can’t be fully present with him at all. My body is sitting in the living room, but my brain is still at the office, or it’s worrying about the mortgage, or it’s panicking about something that hasn’t even happened yet. So, yeah, I’m definitely not participating in my own life the way I used to, let alone enjoying it. It’s just taking a huge toll on everything.
Do you find yourself avoiding social interactions due to feelings of anxiety?

Social interactions? Um... no, not really. I mean, I don't avoid people because I'm anxious about being around them, if that makes sense. It's not like I'm worried they're judging me or that I'm going to say something embarrassing at a party. It's more just... well, like I was saying before, I'm just so incredibly drained by the end of the day. 

So, if someone invites me to happy hour after work, or if a friend wants to get brunch on the weekend, my first thought isn't, "Oh no, what if I make a fool of myself?" My first thought is, "I literally do not have the energy to sit there and pretend to be relaxed while my brain is running through a hundred different worst-case scenarios about next quarter's projections." So I guess I do end up saying no to things, or canceling plans, but it's not because the social interaction itself makes me anxious. It's because the anxiety I already have about everything else just completely exhausts me. 

Like last weekend, my friend Sarah—we've known each other since college—she had this little get-together for her birthday. Nothing crazy, just a few people at her place. And I really wanted to go! I had bought her a gift and everything. But Friday night, after a whole week of stressing over pipeline reports and worrying about whether my top rep was going to jump ship to a competitor, I just... I couldn't do it. I texted her Saturday morning and said I had a migraine. Which, honestly, wasn't entirely a lie, because my head was pounding from all the tension. But the real reason was just that I knew if I went, I wouldn't be able to turn my brain off. I'd be sitting there with a glass of wine, nodding along to whatever story someone was telling, but internally I'd be obsessing over whether I forgot to CC the VP on an email, or if that slight delay in a client's response meant they were pulling out of the deal. It's just not fair to them, and it's exhausting for me. So, no, I don't avoid socializing because I'm scared of socializing. I just avoid it because I don't have any bandwidth left for it.
Do you feel like your anxiety has changed the way you think about yourself?

Changed the way I think about myself? Um... I don't... I'm not really sure what you mean by that, honestly. Like, my self-esteem? I don't think so. I mean, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I still know who I am, you know? I know I'm a smart person, I worked really hard to get my degree and work my way up to sales manager, and I know I have a good track record. 

Deep down, I don't think my actual opinion of myself has changed. I don't sit around thinking I'm a bad person or a failure or anything like that. It's more just... I don't even have the time or the mental space to sit and psychoanalyze my identity because I'm too busy worrying about literally everything else. Like, if I actually have a free second where nobody needs anything from me, my brain isn't going, "Who am I now?" or "Am I a different person?" It's going, "Did I approve that expense report?" or "Is the roof going to leak if it rains this weekend?" or "Did I leave the stove on?" 

So, yeah, I haven't really had any sort of identity crisis or noticed a shift in how I view myself. I'm still just me. I'm just... a really, really exhausted, overwhelmed version of me who can't seem to get a grip on her own thoughts. I might get frustrated with myself for not being able to make a quick decision at work anymore, or for snapping at my husband, but the core of how I think about myself? No, I wouldn't say that's changed. I just haven't really noticed anything like that.
Have you noticed any changes in how you view yourself over the past few months?

I mean... isn't that pretty much what we just talked about? Like I was saying a second ago, I really haven't noticed anything like that. It's not like I look in the mirror and don't recognize the person looking back, or think I'm suddenly incompetent. 

I mean, just last week we had this huge quarterly review, and even though I was an absolute wreck leading up to it—literally sweating through my blouse, double-checking the slide deck maybe fifteen times before the VP even logged onto the Zoom call, just totally convinced I was going to ruin the whole presentation—I still knew, deep down, that I'm a capable manager. I know my worth, I know my education, I know I earned my spot. So, no, my view of myself hasn't really shifted over the last few months at all. 

It's just... the actual experience of being me is a lot harder right now, if that makes sense. Like, the core of who I am is exactly the same as it was six months ago, or a year ago. I'm just buried under this constant avalanche of "what-ifs" and panic about every little detail. But my actual self-esteem? No, that's intact. I just don't have the luxury of sitting around pondering my self-image when I'm too busy worrying if my team is going to hit their quotas or if I forgot to pay the water bill. So yeah, exactly like I said, I haven't noticed any changes in how I view myself. I'm just a very, very tired version of the same person.
Is there any part of your life where you feel completely anxiety-free?

Completely anxiety-free? Um... wow. I wish I could say yes. I really wish I could give you an example, like, 'Oh, I feel totally at peace when I'm watching a movie,' or 'when I'm walking the dog,' but honestly... no. No, I don't think there's a single part of my life right now that isn't touched by it. It's just always there in the background, like this motor that never shuts down, no matter where I am or what I'm doing. 

Most days, my mind just jumps from one potential disaster to the next, even if there isn't an actual crisis happening. Like, I'll be driving to the grocery store, supposedly having a quiet moment to myself, and suddenly I'm obsessing over whether we'll hit the launch numbers for the new product line. And before I can even logic my way through that thought, my brain is already moving on to worry about whether someone on my team is about to quit—maybe because they were a little quiet on our morning stand-up call, or they took an unexpected afternoon off. 

And it doesn't just stop at work stuff, either. It bleeds into my personal life without skipping a beat. So I'll go from stressing about my sales reps, right into panicking about the mortgage, or wondering if that big client renewal is going to fall through at the last second and how that's going to impact our finances. It's like I can't compartmentalize anything anymore. It just feels like every small delay, every little unanswered email or minor hiccup, could turn into something major. If a client takes an extra day to reply, my brain instantly decides they're pulling out of the deal, which means we miss our quota, which means my job is in jeopardy. It's just this constant, exhausting spiral. So... yeah, no. I really don't get a break from it. Whether I'm at my desk, or at the store, or just sitting on my couch on a Sunday afternoon trying to drink a cup of coffee, the worry is just always running.
Do you feel like your anxiety is significantly interfering with your ability to function in your daily life?

I mean... yeah. Honestly, yes. I really didn't want to admit it for a long time, because like I said earlier, I really pride myself on being capable and keeping it together, but... it really is. It's started affecting my work and my home life in ways I just can't ignore anymore. 

At work, it's like... I just spend so much time second-guessing literally every single decision I make. And as a sales manager, I have to make a lot of decisions every day. But lately, I'll just sit there staring at an email or a quarterly forecast, completely paralyzed, wondering if I'm making the wrong call or missing some disastrous detail. It gets to the point where our weekly pipeline reviews—which used to just be standard, run-of-the-mill strategy meetings—they run so incredibly tense now. I'm on edge, I'm grilling my reps over their numbers because I'm terrified a deal is going to fall through, and my team can definitely tell I'm wound up. It just creates this horrible atmosphere in the room where everyone feels like they're walking on eggshells around me. 

And then, because I've spent eight or nine or ten hours in this state of constant high alert, just agonizing over every little detail at the office... by the time I actually get in my car and drive home, I am completely spent. Just totally drained. So when I walk through the front door, I don't have anything left in the tank for my husband. He'll be trying to tell me about his day, or ask a simple question about what we should do for dinner, and I'm just... I'm not fully present with him at all. I'm either completely zoned out, still worrying about a client who didn't email me back, or I'm super reactive and I just snap at him over something ridiculous, like a piece of mail left on the counter. It's not fair to him, and it's really not how I want to be in my marriage, but it's like my brain has just run a marathon all day and I have absolutely no patience or energy left for my actual life. So, yeah, it's definitely interfering.
Have you noticed any changes in your self-confidence since your anxiety started?

Well, I think... honestly, I feel like I've kind of already touched on this a bit, right? I mean, when we were talking earlier about how I view myself, it's pretty much the same thing. My self-confidence itself hasn't really taken a hit, not at its core. Like, I still know I'm good at my job. I know I didn't get to be a sales manager at 32 by accident, you know? I worked incredibly hard for my degree, I grinded through the lower-level positions, I proved myself quarter after quarter. So that foundational belief in my abilities, that hasn't disappeared just because I'm dealing with all this... noise in my head.

But, I guess, if I'm really thinking about it... it's more that the anxiety just makes it so exhausting to access that confidence sometimes. Like, the confidence is there, sitting in a box, but the anxiety has stacked a hundred heavy boxes of "what-ifs" on top of it. So when I'm staring at a forecasting spreadsheet, my brain isn't saying, "You don't know how to do this." It's saying, "What if you missed one tiny variable that throws off the entire projection and ruins the quarter for the whole team?" 

So the self-doubt isn't about my overall competence, it's about the execution in that exact moment. It's like I have to fight through this thick fog of panic just to remind myself that I actually do know what I'm doing. And that's what's so frustrating! I'll be sitting in a meeting, feeling my heart racing, sweating, absolutely convinced I'm about to say the wrong thing and derail a major account, but at the exact same time, there's this logical part of my brain going, "You literally closed three deals exactly like this last year, you know the strategy." 

So, no, I wouldn't say my actual self-confidence has changed or diminished. I don't feel like a lesser person or a failure. It's just... overshadowed, I guess? It's just so much harder to hold onto it when every single minor decision feels like it has life-or-death stakes attached to it. But the confidence itself? Yeah, like I said before, that's still intact. I just wish it didn't feel like such a battle to actually use it every day.
Do you feel like your anxiety is making it difficult for you to maintain relationships with friends and family?

No, actually, I wouldn't say that. My friends and family are... well, they're kind of my anchor, honestly. Like, I know I just talked about how exhausted I am when I get home to my husband, and that's true, but when it comes to my friendships or my parents and my sister... I still show up. I really make it a point to show up. 

For example, my best friend Sarah and I, we've known each other since college, back when we were both pulling all-nighters for our bachelor's degrees, and we still do our every-other-Sunday brunch without fail. Even if I'm sitting there at the restaurant, secretly stressing about a sales forecast or checking my phone under the table to see if a client emailed me back, I'm still there. I don't cancel plans. I think... I think because I'm so used to managing people and managing expectations at work, I just kind of apply that to my social life. I put on my "everything is fine" face and I push through it. 

And it's the same with my family. My mom calls me every Tuesday evening, and I'll pace around the kitchen island for an hour talking to her about her garden or my sister's new job, and I just don't let on how wound up I am. Changed the way I think about myself? Um... I don't... I'm not really sure what you mean by that, honestly. Like, my self-esteem? I don't think so. Like, if I actually have a free second where nobody needs anything from me, my brain isn't going, "Who am I now?" or "Am I a different person?" It's going, "Did I approve that expense report?" or "Is the roof going to leak if it rains this weekend?" or "Did I leave the stove on?" 

So, yeah, I haven't really had any sort of identity crisis or noticed a shift in how I view myself. I'm still just me. I'm just... a really, really exhausted, overwhelmed version of me who can't seem to get a grip on her own thoughts. I might get frustrated with myself for not being able to make a quick decision at work anymore, or for snapping at my husband, but the core of how I think about myself? No, I wouldn't say that's changed. I just haven't really noticed anything like that.

patient.answer:
Completely anxiety-free? Um... wow. I wish I could say yes. I really wish I could give you an example, like, 'Oh, I feel totally at peace when I'm watching a movie,' or 'when I'm walking the dog,' but honestly... no. No, I don't think there's a single part of my life right now that isn't touched by it. It's just always there in the background, like this motor that never shuts down, no matter where I am or what I'm doing. 

Most days, my mind just jumps from one potential disaster to the next, even if there isn't an actual crisis happening. Like, I'll be driving to the grocery store, supposedly having a quiet moment to myself, and suddenly I'm obsessing over whether we'll hit the launch numbers for the new product line. And before I can even logic my way through that thought, my brain is already moving on to worry about whether someone on my team is about to quit—maybe because they were a little quiet on our morning stand-up call, or they took an unexpected afternoon off. 

And it doesn't just stop at work stuff, either. It bleeds into my personal life without skipping a beat. So I'll go from stressing about my sales reps, right into panicking about the mortgage, or wondering if that big client renewal is going to fall through at the last second and how that's going to impact our finances. It's like I can't compartmentalize anything anymore. It just feels like every small delay, every little unanswered email or minor hiccup, could turn into something major. If a client takes an extra day to reply, my brain instantly decides they're pulling out of the deal, which means we miss our quota, which means my job is in jeopardy. It's just this constant, exhausting spiral. So... yeah, no. I really don't get a break from it. Whether I'm at my desk, or at the store, or just sitting on my couch on a Sunday afternoon trying to drink a cup of coffee, the worry is just always running.

I mean... yeah. Honestly, yes. I really didn't want to admit it for a long time, because like I said earlier, I really pride myself on being capable and keeping it together, but... it really is. It's started affecting my work and my home life in ways I just can't ignore anymore. 

At work, it's like... I just spend so much time second-guessing literally every single decision I make. And as a sales manager, I have to make a lot of decisions every day. But lately, I'll just sit there staring at an email or a quarterly forecast, completely paralyzed, wondering if I'm making the wrong call or missing some disastrous detail. It gets to the point where our weekly pipeline reviews—which used to just be standard, run-of-the-mill strategy meetings—they run so incredibly tense now. I'm on edge, I'm grilling my reps over their numbers because I'm terrified a deal is going to fall through, and my team can definitely tell I'm wound up. It just creates this horrible atmosphere in the room where everyone feels like they're walking on eggshells around me. 

And then, because I've spent eight or nine or ten hours in this state of constant high alert, just agonizing over every little detail at the office... by the time I actually get in my car and drive home, I am completely spent. Just totally drained. So when I walk through the front door, I don't have anything left in the tank for my husband. He'll be trying to tell me about his day, or ask a simple question about what we should do for dinner, and I'm just... I'm not fully present with him at all. I'm either completely zoned out, still worrying about a client who didn't email me back, or I'm super reactive and I just snap at him over something ridiculous, like a piece of mail left on the counter. It's not fair to him, and it's really not how I want to be in my marriage, but it's like my brain has just run a marathon all day and I have absolutely no patience or energy left for my actual life. So, yeah, it's definitely interfering.

My self-confidence itself hasn't really taken a hit, not at its core. Like, I still know I'm good at my job. I know I didn't get to be a sales manager at 32 by accident, you know? I worked incredibly hard for my degree, I grinded through the lower-level positions, I proved myself quarter after quarter. So that foundational belief in my abilities, that hasn't disappeared just because I'm dealing with all this... noise in my head.

But, I guess, if I'm really thinking about it... it's more that the anxiety just makes it so exhausting to access that confidence sometimes. Like, the confidence is there, sitting in a box, but the anxiety has stacked a hundred heavy boxes of "what-ifs" on top of it. So when I'm staring at a forecasting spreadsheet, my brain isn't saying, "You don't know how to do this." It's saying, "What if you missed one tiny variable that throws off the entire projection and ruins the quarter for the whole team?" 

So the self-doubt isn't about my overall competence, it's about the execution in that exact moment. It's like I have to fight through this thick fog of panic just to remind myself that I actually do know what I'm doing. And that's what's so frustrating! I'll be sitting in a meeting, feeling my heart racing, sweating, absolutely convinced I'm about to say the wrong thing and derail a major account, but at the exact same time, there's this logical part of my brain going, "You literally closed three deals exactly like this last year, you know the strategy." 

So, no, I wouldn't say my actual self-confidence has changed or diminished. I don't feel like a lesser person or a failure. It's just... overshadowed, I guess? It's just so much harder to hold onto it when every single minor decision feels like it has life-or-death stakes attached to it. But the confidence itself? Yeah, like I said before, that's still intact. I just wish it didn't feel like such a battle to actually use it every day.

No, actually, I wouldn't say that. My friends and family are... well, they're kind of my anchor, honestly. Like, I know I just talked about how exhausted I am when I get home to my husband, and that's true, but when it comes to my friendships or my parents and my sister... I still show up. I really make it a point to show up. 

For example, my best friend Sarah and I, we've known each other since college, back when we were both pulling all-nighters for our bachelor's degrees, and we still do our every-other-Sunday brunch without fail. Even if I'm sitting there at the restaurant, secretly stressing about a sales forecast or checking my phone under the table to see if a client emailed me back, I'm still there. I don't cancel plans. I think... I think because I'm so used to managing people and managing expectations at work, I just kind of apply that to my social life. Like I said, sometimes my mind is a million miles away worrying about our quarterly quota when Sarah is trying to tell me about her dating life, but I always make sure to nod and ask the right questions so she feels heard. I'm very careful about that.

My husband and I have a beautiful home that we actually just spent the last two years renovating—mostly the kitchen, because I love to cook, or at least I did before work got so intense. We put in this huge farmhouse sink and these gorgeous quartz countertops that I spent literal weeks agonizing over the exact shade of white for... which, looking back, might have been the worrying kicking into high gear, but anyway. We have the house. I have a job that pays very well, I have my degree, I have Sarah and my family. We still go on our annual trip to my parents' lake house every August without fail. 

So, on paper, my quality of life is fantastic. Someone looking at my life from the outside, or just talking to me at a neighborhood barbecue, would think I have it all completely figured out. So no, I wouldn't say this is ruining my quality of life. It's not like I'm miserable or unable to get out of bed in the morning. I still enjoy a good glass of Pinot Noir on the patio, I still laugh at my husband's terrible jokes—when I have the energy for them, like I mentioned earlier. 

It's just... it's more like there's this constant background static. Like a radio left on in the other room just slightly too loud. It doesn't stop me from living my life or enjoying the big moments, but it's just always *there*, making everything take a little more effort. But "significantly impacting"?
